description:
We are a team of five curious and motivated participants from Kazakhstan with different backgrounds and skills, united by our interest in space, science, technology, and solving real-world problems.

Our team brings together experience and interests in IT, mathematics, physics, research, robotics, design, and communication. We enjoy exploring new ideas, learning from one another, and turning complex challenges into practical solutions.
summary: AEROCORE lets an astronaut check their own aerobic fitness — which NASA requires to stay at or above 80% of the pre-flight level — without waiting for Earth or a 3-hour maximal test. The astronaut does the short cycle test already used on the ISS. AEROCORE checks the data (it catches impossible values and recording errors), estimates fitness with NASA's own method against the astronaut's personal baseline, and says what to do: carry on, schedule a full test, or tell the flight surgeon before a spacewalk. We tested the rule on NASA bed-rest data (LSDA MR080G): the short test alone would falsely flag 26% of fit crew, but used as a screen it catches 99% of breaches with 2.2 maximal tests per 180-day mission instead of 4.9 under monthly maximal testing (simulation built on the NASA data). A flight-surgeon view shows the whole crew, and the data checks found 12 kinds of recording errors in the public NASA archive.
details:
THE PROBLEM

NASA-STD-3001 [V1 4003] requires each astronaut to keep VO₂max at or above 80% of the pre-mission value, measured directly or indirectly. On the ISS about half of crew members lose more than 10% and 15% lose more than 20% (NASA HRP Evidence Report). The direct measurement is a maximal cycle test: exhausting and time-consuming — in NASA's ISS VO₂max study each in-flight session took about 3 hours including setup — and harder still on exploration missions with less crew time and equipment. Routinely, ISS crews do a short submaximal test (the Periodic Fitness Evaluation) about monthly, from which NASA estimates aerobic capacity (ACI). But NASA's own investigators reported that submaximal techniques do not track measured VO₂max well (Moore 2010). The open question is how to use that routine test safely for the 80% decision.

WHAT AEROCORE DOES

The challenge asks for software that gathers health indicators and lets astronauts evaluate and act on their own health. AEROCORE does this for aerobic fitness, the indicator NASA guards with a numeric standard.

- Astronaut view (main screen): the astronaut enters or loads the short cycle test (three stages, heart rate and VO₂). AEROCORE checks the data, shows estimated fitness as % of their own pre-flight level on a chart of how the estimate is made, and gives one plain action: carry on, schedule a full test and tell the flight surgeon, or do the full test before any spacewalk planning.

- Confirmation: the full-test result can be revealed for each check, so every decision is tested against the truth (in the NASA study the full test was done the same day).

- Two modes: replay real NASA participants, or enter my own numbers and save checks to build a personal trend. "Send to flight surgeon" turns any check into a plain-text report; a glossary explains every term.

- Flight-surgeon view: every crew member against their own baseline — measured peak VO₂ coloured green (≥ 85%), amber (80–85%) or red (below the NASA standard), with the short-test estimate under it.

- Screening rule: ACI every 14 days; when ACI falls below 85% of baseline, AEROCORE orders a maximal (Peak) test to confirm.

- Every flag is explained (for example, a peak heart rate that fell more than 10 bpm, meaning the test may not have been maximal).

- Every data file is checked before analysis: units, impossible values, swapped or shifted columns, duplicated tests, conflicting dates, NASA maximal-effort criteria. Raw values are never silently changed.

- Runs in any browser from one file. Teams can load their own CSV files; nothing leaves the computer.

HOW IT WORKS

- Data trust layer: column recognition, unit detection, range and consistency checks (e.g. VCO₂/VO₂ must match RER; mass computed from VO₂ and VO₂/kg must match the recorded mass), duplicate and conflict detection across files, header and date cross-checks.

- Personal baseline: mean of pre-mission tests in the same body posture; change judged against measurement error, not a fixed percentage.

- ACI as NASA computes it: heart rate regressed on VO₂ over submaximal stages and extrapolated to the person's pre-mission peak heart rate (Moore 2015).

- Evidence: real NASA data (MR080G Campaign 3, 60–90-day bed rest; CFT70, 70-day bed rest), 95% confidence intervals by bootstrap over participants, and a 20,000-person virtual crew over 180 days to compare monitoring protocols, re-run under 18 changed assumptions. Protocol numbers (99%, 2.2 vs 4.9) come from this simulation, with its parameters taken from the NASA data.

WHAT WE FOUND ON NASA DATA (95% CI in brackets)

- Peak VO₂ at the end of 60–90-day bed rest (median, 15 people): −32% [−37; −25]

- Peak heart rate change (key ACI assumption): −0.3 [−2.3; +1.5] bpm — stable

- ACI follows the measured change: r = 0.74 [0.62; 0.89]

- Noise of a single ACI test: 6.4% [4.2; 8.1]

- ACI alone, single test: 26% false alarms among fit crew

- Screen (ACI every 14 d → Peak if < 85%) vs Peak every 30 d (simulation): catches 99% vs 98% of breaches; 2.2 vs 4.9 maximal tests per 180-day mission

- Robustness (simulation): within 0.5 point of monthly testing in 15 of 18 scenarios; 25–78% fewer maximal tests

- "Below 80%" decision by ACI on real tests: caught 9 of 10; correctly cleared 9 of 11

- CFT70, below 80% right after bed rest: control 5/8, exercise 0/18, flywheel 0/8; change differs between control and exercise groups (Mann–Whitney p = 0.0002)

- ACI bias depends on protocol: NASA stepped test −6.2%, ramp tests (PhysioNet) +4.0%

- Learning effect between two pre-tests: +5.1% [1.9; 9.2]; changes the 80% decision for 5 of 29 tests

Honest baseline: within one homogeneous bed-rest cohort, ACI is no more accurate than assuming everyone loses the cohort average (6.6 vs 6.8 percentage points). That average does not transfer — applied to the CFT70 exercise and flywheel groups it errs by 27 points. ACI is therefore a personal screen, and the maximal test makes the decision.

Data trust: all 1,505 MR080G files match NASA's own MD5 checksums, yet the archive contains 12 kinds of recording errors, among them mass and height swapped, heights entered in inches, a file whose header was copied from another visit (it would put one person twice at the same time point), rotated columns, and heart rate 0 at an exercise stage. One of them silently distorted our own first analysis before the checks caught it.

BENEFITS

- Crew time: in the simulation, 2.2 instead of 4.9 maximal tests per crew member per 180-day mission, with the same detection.

- Safety: a breach is confirmed by a maximal test, and the data says to repeat it — a maximal test itself varies about 5.5% between repeats.

- Trustworthy data: errors are caught before they reach a fitness-for-duty decision.

- Transparency: every flag shows its reason, the NASA standard behind it and the source.

INTENDED IMPACT

- ISS: fewer maximal tests with the same protection of the 80% standard.

- Artemis and Mars: a decision tool where a full maximal test is not always possible.

- Analog studies: data checks before analysis.

Next steps: validate the screen on ISS flight records (NASA PFE and VO₂max studies) and Artemis analog campaigns; offer the data checks to NASA's Life Sciences Data Archive for incoming datasets; calibrate the screening threshold with NASA flight surgeons and exercise physiologists.

CREATIVITY

Instead of trying to make the submaximal estimate replace the maximal test, AEROCORE uses it as a personal screen that decides when the maximal test is needed — and proves the trade-off on NASA data with a virtual crew. It also treats data quality as part of crew safety: the same checks that protect the astronaut's decision found 12 kinds of errors in a public NASA archive.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (single offline file, SVG charts); Python 3 with pandas, NumPy, SciPy and matplotlib for the analysis; Node.js for tests and build; Playwright with Chrome for interface checks; GitHub Pages for hosting. AI assistance is disclosed in the repository README and in code metadata.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED / LIMITATIONS

- Bed rest is a ground analog of spaceflight; flight data are needed to confirm the result.

- ACI was computed from the 3-minute stages at the start of each maximal test, not from a separate submaximal session (the ISS test uses 5-minute stages).

- The 85% screening threshold and the 14-day interval are our proposal, not NASA's.

- Reaching 80% alone does not establish spacewalk readiness; NASA also sets absolute EVA requirements.

- AEROCORE is a research prototype, not a medical device.

LINKS

Source code, analysis scripts and data manifest: https://github.com/marzhannurbakyt/aerocore
